explanations.explanation: Egypt it is. The angel says, “Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt.” Joseph gets the whole plan in a dream, and the place is named right there. No guessing and no wrong turns, just get up and go.

Babylon never comes up in this passage, friend. The angel says, “…flee to Egypt.” I think Babylon is an easy name to grab because you may have seen it elsewhere in your Bible reading. Here the angel gives one place, and it's Egypt.
Damascus is a real city, but this angel never says it. The words are “…flee to Egypt.” Joseph's directions would fit on a cookie box lid: one word, no turns. Egypt.

Close, because Herod did say something like that. He told the Magi, “…so that I too may go and worship Him.” (Matthew 2:8) But the angel tells Joseph what Herod, the king (Matthew 2:1), is really going to do. Herod is going to search for the Child to kill Him.

That's right. The angel says Herod is going to search for the Child “…to kill Him.” Herod, the king (Matthew 2:1), had told the Magi he wanted to worship Him (Matthew 2:8). The angel gives Joseph the truth, and Joseph hears it in the middle of a dream.

By night. Joseph gets up, takes the Child and His mother, and withdraws to Egypt while it's dark. Me, I once waited for a more convenient time to start a batch and the dough sat there for a week. Joseph just moves.
Sunrise is a nice guess, but Matthew says Joseph took them “by night.” He doesn't wait around for the sun to come up. The angel said to get up, and Joseph gets up.
Noon is the middle of the day, and Matthew has a different time. He says Joseph took the Child and His mother “by night.” So the family is already on the move in the dark.

Death is the word. Joseph stayed in Egypt until the death of Herod. Matthew then says this fulfilled what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called My Son.” The family stays put until that point.
Pardon sounds polite, but nobody pardons anybody here. Matthew says Joseph stayed in Egypt until the death of Herod. Herod's rage in this passage doesn't end with a pardon.
Defeat sounds like a battle, and no army shows up in these verses. Matthew says Joseph stayed in Egypt until the death of Herod. It's one word, and it's death.

Rage. Matthew says Herod saw he had been outwitted by the Magi and “…he was filled with rage.” That's a big word, and Matthew picked it. The orders he sends in that same verse are the heavy part of this story.
Sorrow is a gentle guess, but it's not the word Matthew uses for Herod. He says Herod was filled with rage. The sorrow shows up a few verses later, in the weeping of Rachel.
I think shame is a natural guess when someone gets outwitted. Matthew says something different, though: Herod was filled with rage. Nothing in the text says Herod felt ashamed.

explanations.answer: The time he learned from the Magi
explanations.explanation: That's right. Herod acted “…according to the time he had learned from the Magi.” Earlier he had called the Magi in secret and found out from them the exact time the star appeared (Matthew 2:7). That's where the age came from.

explanations.answer: A word from the chief priests
explanations.explanation: Herod did gather the chief priests and scribes, but he asked them where the Christ was to be born (Matthew 2:4). Their answer was Bethlehem (Matthew 2:5-6). The age came from somewhere else, “…the time he had learned from the Magi.”
Matthew says Herod sent orders, but he never mentions a report from soldiers. The text says he acted “…according to the time he had learned from the Magi.” That time came from the Magi themselves.

True. Matthew quotes Jeremiah: “…Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.” I think this one hurts. It's a heavy part of the story, and Matthew doesn't skip it.

It's actually true, friend. The words from Jeremiah say Rachel is “…weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.” I think this is one of the hardest lines in the passage. It's a sad moment, and I'd rather say so than rush past it.
Israel. The angel says, “Take the Child and His mother and go to the land of Israel…” Joseph is in Egypt when the dream comes. Now he knows which way to point the family.
Moab doesn't show up anywhere in the angel's words. The angel says, “…go to the land of Israel…” It's an easy name to grab if you know your Old Testament. Here, though, the answer is Israel.
Edom never comes up in this dream. The angel tells Joseph, “…go to the land of Israel…” That's the land named in the angel's words. Edom's out.

explanations.answer: Those seeking the Child's life are dead
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the angel gives. He says, “…for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead.” Herod's death is the point where the angel sends Joseph home. Back in Matthew 2:13, Joseph heard stay in Egypt until I tell you, and now the word is go.

explanations.answer: Egypt is no longer safe for them
explanations.explanation: The angel never says anything about Egypt being unsafe. His reason is “…for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead.” That's the whole reason he gives. I'd stick with what he says.

explanations.answer: The people of Israel are asking for Him
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, but nobody in Israel is asking for Him in this passage. The angel says, “…for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead.” That's the reason the angel gives to Joseph. No crowds and no invitations, just the news that those seeking the Child's life are dead.

Afraid is the word Matthew uses. Joseph learns that Archelaus, Herod's son, is reigning in Judea in place of his father, and he is afraid to go there. Matthew gives us that fear straight from the text. And then comes another dream.

Eager sounds like a happy homecoming. Matthew says something else: when Joseph learns Archelaus is reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, “…he was afraid to go there.” So Joseph doesn't head that way.
Proud is not the feeling Matthew gives. He says Joseph “…was afraid to go there.” Archelaus is Herod's son, and he is reigning in Judea in place of his father.

True. Matthew says Joseph was “…warned in a dream…” and then he withdrew to the district of Galilee. That's the third dream in the passage, after the two where an angel of the Lord appears. And Joseph acts on this one too.

It's true, friend. Matthew says, “…having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the district of Galilee…” That's another dream in this passage, after the two where an angel of the Lord appears. Joseph is getting a lot of directions in his dreams.

Nazareth. Joseph went and lived in a town called Nazareth, in the district of Galilee. Matthew says this was so “He will be called a Nazarene.” was fulfilled. That name goes with the town where the family lands.

Capernaum is a real town in Galilee, but it's not the one here. Matthew says Joseph went and lived in a town called Nazareth. Jesus does go to live in Capernaum later (Matthew 4:13), just not in this passage.
Bethsaida is a real place, I'll give you that. But Matthew says Joseph lived in a town called Nazareth. That's the town in this passage.
